unit.title: Prepare customer accounts and deal with departures

summary: This unit teaches you to get a guest's bill ready and to check the guest out smoothly: prepare for the day's departures, check folios and vouchers the night before, present the bill, take payment in cash, card or US$, handle company and group accounts, deal with disputes, late check-outs and guests who leave without paying, and finish the departure by clearing the room status, storing luggage and keeping records.

blocks.p: Check-out is the last thing the guest remembers. A guest who has had a lovely stay can leave annoyed because of a wrong bill or a long wait at the desk. A guest who had a few problems can leave happy if check-out is quick, fair and friendly. For the property, check-out is also when the money is collected, so every mistake in the account shows up here.

This unit is for HOSPITALITY VILLA/PROPERTIES SERVICES LEVEL 2 trainees who work at the front desk or in the office of a villa, guest house or hotel. It follows on from keeping guests' accounts during the stay, and it covers the **departure**: getting the bill ready, settling it, and finishing the guest's visit.

What this means at the front desk

Use the departures list and the night's checks

Arrange luggage help, transport and wake-up calls
Prepare each guest's bill
Check the folio against signed vouchers
Make sure deposits, company arrangements and late charges are dealt with
Check the guest out
Confirm identity, present the folio, take payment, give a receipt
Collect the key card and thank the guest
Take payment correctly
Cash, card, US$ at the property's rate, part payments
Company, group and all-inclusive accounts

Declined cards, guests who do not come to the desk, guests who leave without paying

Update the room status and tell housekeeping

flow: Departures list and night checks
Prepare folios and vouchers
Greet and confirm the guest
Present the folio and agree it
Take payment and give a receipt
Collect the key; arrange luggage and transport
Thank the guest; update room status and records

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice questions, short answers and essays) and practical tasks in the Centre's mock front desk. In the tasks you prepare and check made-up folios for tomorrow's departures, then check out guests in role plays and deal with departure problems. The assessor watches your accuracy, your checking, your manner and your care with private information.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: Use only made-up folios, made-up money (marked TRAINING) and made-up exchange rates in practice. Never use a real guest's details.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: The **departures list** is a report that shows which guests are due to leave today: names, rooms, times, how they will pay, and any special notes. The desk uses it to plan the morning.

head: Check on the list
What you do with it
rows: Names and room numbers
Print or open each guest's folio.
How each guest will pay
Card, cash, company, tour operator. Make sure you have what you need (a company letter, a card hold).
Flight or departure times
Plan which guests to check out first; arrange transport and luggage help.
Late check-out or luggage storage requests
Check room availability and the property's policy; reply to the guest.
Special notes
A VIP, a complaint, a birthday, or a message for the guest.
Stayovers (guests staying on)
Do not check these guests out; keep the two groups apart.

blocks.p: On the evening before a guest leaves, the desk checks the guest's folio. This is done so that **mistakes are fixed before the guest is at the desk**, not when the guest is waiting with a flight to catch.

flow: Print or open the folios of the guests leaving tomorrow
Check each charge against the signed slip or voucher (restaurant, bar, spa, laundry, tours)
Look for common mistakes: a wrong room number, a charge posted twice, a missing signature, a wrong amount
Fix errors with the proper approvals (see the unit on keeping guests' accounts)
Check deposits and card holds are linked, and that company or tour billing letters are in the folder
Tell departments to send in their slips early, to avoid late charges
Prepare each folio, sorted in order of departure time

head: Voucher problem
What to do
rows: Wrong room number on the slip
Find out the right guest from the department; move the charge with a recorded correction.
No signature
Ask the department whether the guest signed; do not post without a signature unless policy allows.
A charge posted twice
Post an adjustment for the duplicate; keep the reason.
Amount differs from the slip
Post an adjustment for the difference.
A slip with no folio match (the guest has checked out)
This is a **late charge**: report it and follow the policy.

blocks.p: A **late charge** is a charge that reaches the desk after the guest has checked out. It is common with the **minibar**, breakfast, the bar and the spa.

ul: At check-out, ask the guest: 'Have you had anything from the minibar, or breakfast this morning, or any other charges?'
Ask housekeeping to check the minibar before the guest leaves, if that is the property's practice.
Ask departments to send slips straight away, especially for early departures.
Keep a note of the guest's card on file with the guest's signed permission, so that a late charge can be dealt with by policy.
**Wake-up calls** for early flights, booked and confirmed.

**Transport**: a pre-booked airport transfer or a taxi. For visitors flying out, Sangster International Airport (Montego Bay) and Norman Manley International Airport (Kingston) are the two main airports. Allow plenty of time, because traffic and roadworks can slow the journey.
**Luggage help**: a bell attendant with a trolley, for guests with heavy bags.
**Packed breakfast** for a very early departure, if the property offers it.
**Express check-out**: the guest pays by card on file without queueing at the desk, and the folio is sent to them. Use it only when the guest has agreed and the property's policy allows.

blocks.note: In the hurricane season (June to November), flights can be cancelled or delayed. A guest may need to stay longer or leave early. Tell your supervisor at once and follow the property's plan: do not decide room changes or rate changes yourself.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: Preparing and checking the guest's bill

head: Part
What it shows
rows: Guest details
Name, room, arrival and departure dates, folio number.
Charges
Room charges for each night, taxes (GCT) and any service charge, restaurant, bar, minibar, laundry, spa, tours, paid-outs.
Payments
Deposits, card holds that have become payments, payments already made during the stay.
Allowances and adjustments
Any corrections, with reasons.
Balance
Total charges minus total payments: the amount owing at check-out.

blocks.p: A guest's account is settled when the balance is **zero (J$0.00)**.

ul: A **deposit** the guest paid when booking is a payment. At check-out it is **taken off** the amount owed.
A **pre-authorisation** is a hold on the guest's card put on at check-in to cover charges. It is not a payment. At check-out you charge the card for the balance, and the hold is released.
If the deposit is larger than the charges, the property owes the guest a **refund**, to be made as policy says (usually to the same card or in the same way it was paid).

blocks.p: Ms Pauline Gordon stayed 4 nights at J$15,000 a night, and had a meal J$6,800, a boat trip J$9,500, minibar J$1,200 and laundry J$2,500. She paid a J$20,000 deposit.

head: Item
Charges (J$)
Payments (J$)
rows: Meal
Boat trip
Minibar
Laundry
Deposit
Totals

blocks.p: Balance = 80,000 − 20,000 = **J$60,000**. Add the charges in two different orders to check, and check that the deposit was taken off.

head: Kind of account
What happens at check-out
rows: Guest pays everything
One folio; the guest checks it and pays.
Company pays everything (by invoice later)
Check the company's **written approval**. Send the folio to the **city ledger**. The guest signs the folio to confirm the charges.
Company pays the room only; guest pays the extras
**Two folios**, one for each payer. The company's folio goes to the city ledger; the guest checks and pays the personal folio.
Tour group, where the tour company pays for rooms (a **master folio**)
The master folio goes to the tour company. Each group member settles their own extras, such as drinks and spa.
All-inclusive package
The package covers the room, meals and some drinks. The guest still pays at check-out for **extras outside the package**, such as the spa, special tours and premium drinks.
Prepaid by an agent or website
Check what was paid and what was not (taxes, extras). The guest pays the difference.

blocks.note: Never charge a company until you hold its written approval. If a guest says 'my company is paying' and you cannot find the letter, ask your supervisor before you check the guest out.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: **GCT (General Consumption Tax)** is a tax on sales, shown on the folio at the **current rate set by law**. If a guest asks why it is on the bill, explain politely that it is the tax on goods and services and that the property is required to collect it. Never use a rate you remember or invent one: use the rate shown by the system or by your supervisor.

flow: Greet the guest with a smile, by name if you know it
Confirm which room they are in: ask for their name and **key card**, quietly, without saying the room number aloud
Ask if they have had any charges today (the minibar, breakfast, the bar)
Give the guest the folio and ask them to check it
Explain any charge if asked, and deal with queries
Ask how they would like to pay, and take payment
Give a **receipt** or a copy of the settled folio
Collect the key card and any other keys, and check the safe deposit box
Offer luggage help or transport, and ask about their stay
Thank the guest by name and invite them back

head: Step
Why you do it
rows: Confirm the room quietly
So you open the right folio and nobody overhears the room number.
Ask about last-minute charges
Prevents late charges.
Give the guest the folio to check **before** they pay
So they agree the charges are correct, and disagreements are settled before money changes hands.
Give a receipt or settled folio
It proves the guest has paid, and the balance is zero.
Ask for the key card back
For the room's security, and so that it can be re-used.
Check the safe deposit box
Make sure the guest's valuables have been taken out and the key returned.
Ask for feedback
To learn what the guest liked and what to improve; offer a comment card.
Thank by name and invite back
The last impression decides whether the guest returns.

ul: Check-out is a busy time: several guests may arrive together. Greet each one with eye contact and a smile, even if you are serving someone else: 'I will be with you in a moment.'
Be quick but accurate. A mistake costs more time than taking an extra minute to check.
Speak quietly about money, and never discuss one guest's bill within another guest's hearing.
Use the guest's name, and speak with warmth, even when you are tired.

blocks.p: Some guests use **express check-out**: they agree to pay by the card on file, and do not queue at the desk. The folio is emailed to them or left for collection.

ul: Check that the guest has agreed in writing, and that a card is on file.
Check the folio before you charge it, as for any other check-out.
Send the folio afterwards, and answer questions quickly if the guest disagrees with a charge.

blocks.h: What if the guest does not come to the desk?

ul: If a guest on today's departures list has not come by check-out time, **call the room politely** to check their plans: they may have forgotten, be ill or want to stay longer.
Never enter the room yourself. Ask housekeeping or a supervisor to follow the property's procedure.
Do not assume the guest has left without paying. Report your worry to the supervisor.

head: Way of paying
What you do
What you check
rows: Card
Key the amount into the terminal
Hand the terminal to the guest for the PIN or signature
Give back the card and print a receipt
The amount keyed is exactly the amount owed
The terminal says approved
The name and card match the guest, as policy says
Cash (J$)
Count it with the guest, post it, give change and a receipt
The notes are genuine, as the property's check says
Change is correct
Cash (US$)
Convert at the property's rate for the day
Post the J$ value, give change in J$ unless policy says otherwise, give a receipt showing the rate
Use the **property's rate for that day**, not another
Part cash, part card
Take the cash first and post it, then charge the card for the rest
The two amounts add up to the balance
Company or tour operator
Check the written approval; send to the city ledger; the guest signs the folio
The approval covers these charges
Deposit used
Take the deposit off, then collect any balance
The deposit was posted and is not counted twice

blocks.p: Guests often pay in US dollars. The property sets a **rate each day**. Multiply US$ by the rate to get J$; divide J$ by the rate to get US$.

head: Example (made-up rate US$1 = J$150)
Working
Answer
rows: A folio of J$30,000 paid in US$ cash
US$120 paid towards a bill
A J$45,000 bill, guest pays US$200 cash, the rest by card
J$15,000 by card

ul: Check that the decimal point is right: US$200 at 150 is J$30,000, not J$3,000 or J$300,000.
Show the US$ received, the rate and the J$ credited on the receipt and the folio.
The rates in this kit are made up for practice. In real work, use the property's rate for that day.
Tell the guest **quietly and privately**; never announce it in the lobby.
Ask for another card or another way to pay. Do not try the card again and again.
If the guest cannot pay, call your supervisor. Do not let the guest leave with the problem unsolved.
Keep cash in the drawer, never in your pocket. Lock the drawer when you leave the desk.
Count large amounts away from other guests' view.
Never leave the drawer open, and do not let anyone else use it.
If your drawer does not balance at the end of the shift, report it. Do not try to hide it.

blocks.note: A settled folio has a balance of J$0.00. If it does not, find out why before the guest leaves the desk.
blocks.label: Remember

flow: Stay calm and listen to the whole complaint
Check the **signed voucher** with the guest, privately
If the voucher shows the guest's signature, explain it politely
If the charge is wrong, apologise and correct it: an allowance needs the **supervisor's** approval
If you cannot settle it, call the supervisor
Record what was decided

ul: Never tell the guest 'the system is never wrong'. The guest may be right.
Never take a charge off without approval. An allowance is approved by the supervisor.
Do not argue. Try to end with the guest satisfied, even if the charge stands.

blocks.p: A guest may say at check-out that the air conditioning was noisy all week. This is useful information, and you should be glad to receive it.

ul: **Apologise** sincerely, thank the guest for telling you, and do not make excuses.
**Record** it, and tell maintenance or the supervisor so that it is fixed before the next guest.
Let the supervisor decide whether an allowance or a gesture is right.

blocks.p: Check-out time is the time by which guests must leave the room (often late morning). A guest may ask to keep the room longer, for example for an afternoon flight.

ul: Check the **room availability** (is another guest arriving soon?) and the **property's policy** (a late check-out may be free for a short time, or charged).
Reply politely and tell the guest the cost, if any, **before** they agree.
If you cannot give a late check-out, offer to store the luggage and let the guest use the public areas.
Tell housekeeping, so that they plan the room.

A guest who has checked out may leave bags at the property until the afternoon. **Tag them** with the guest's name, count them and write the number on the tag and the log, and keep them in the **luggage room**, which is locked.
Give the guest the claim tag. When they return, check the tag and have them sign.
Do not store valuables, cash or perishable food, as the property's policy says.

blocks.p: A guest who booked five nights and wants to leave after three has an **early departure**. Check the booking terms for early departure: there may be a charge. Do not decide yourself: tell the supervisor. Also update the room status and the reservation.
A guest who leaves without paying is called a **skipper**.

ul: If you think a guest may have left without paying, **report it to your supervisor at once**.
Do not chase the guest, accuse anyone, or discuss it in public.
The supervisor decides what to do. Write an incident report.
Get the group's check-out list and departure time before the day.
Settle each person's extras separately and quickly. The tour company pays the rooms (master folio).
Have all folios ready, tagged luggage in the lobby and key folders ready to collect.
Meet the tour leader, so that the group leaves on time.

Change the room's status to **vacant dirty (VD)** and tell housekeeping at once. They can clean the room and put it back on sale. If it stays unreported, the room cannot be sold and a new guest may be kept waiting.
Tell housekeeping about any special needs: a guest's lost property, a fault, extra cleaning.
Check the keys: all room keys and key cards returned. If one is missing, report it so the lock can be reset.
Check the safe deposit box is empty and the key is returned.
Update the **guest history**: likes and needs noted for the next stay, any complaint and how it was settled.
File the signed folio, vouchers and receipts, as the property says.
Write the **log book** at the end of each shift: late charges to follow up, guests who owe money, items in the luggage room, anything the next shift must know.
Keep records private. Do not leave folios on the desk.

blocks.p: At the end of your shift, tell the next shift what is unfinished. A log book that is clear and complete means a guest's problem is not forgotten. Hand over the cash drawer, keys and folios, and check the amounts with the next person.

head: Situation
What you do
rows: A caller says they are the guest's friend and asks you to read out the bill
Politely refuse and offer to take a message.
A person asks for a copy of a folio that is not theirs
Refuse; only the guest whose folio it is may have it.
A guest asks you to email the folio to their company
Do it only with the guest's clear permission, and to the address they give you at the desk.
A visitor asks where a guest is going
Say you cannot give information about guests.

blocks.note: A folio holds private details: names, spending, card information. Print it or show it only to the guest who owns it.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Guests judge their stay by how it begins and how it ends. A warm, efficient departure turns a good stay into a great one and a mixed stay into a forgiven one.

head: Do
Avoid
rows: Smile and greet by name
Looking at the screen and not at the guest
Have the folio ready and checked
Making the guest wait while you find the bill
Ask about the stay, and listen
Rushing the guest because there is a queue
Offer luggage help and transport
Leaving a guest with heavy bags to carry
Apologise for any problem, and fix it
Blaming another department or the guest
Thank the guest and invite them back
Saying nothing as the guest walks out

ul: Offer a **comment card** and ask for feedback; it shows you care and gives the property useful information.
A guest who leaves a short, polite note about something good can be recorded in the guest history and shared with the team.
If a guest is upset, let the supervisor or manager speak to them before they leave.

blocks.note: In Jamaica a warm farewell, such as 'Come back soon, and walk good', is part of the welcome the island is known for. Use the words that suit you and your property.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: I can use the departures list to plan the day's check-outs.
I can check folios the night before against signed vouchers and fix errors.
I can explain how to prevent and deal with late charges.
I can work out a final balance, taking off deposits, and explain a pre-authorisation.
I can set up the right bill for a guest, a company, a split account, a tour group or an all-inclusive guest.
I can check a guest out step by step: confirm, present the folio, take payment, give a receipt, collect the key.
I can take payment by cash, card, US$ at the property's rate, or part by each.
I can deal with a declined card, a disputed charge, a complaint and an early departure.
I can handle a late check-out and store luggage safely.
I know what to do if a guest does not come to the desk or may have left without paying.
I can change the room status to VD and tell housekeeping, and I know why it matters.
I can keep records, write the log, and protect the guest's privacy.
I can leave the guest with a good last impression.

terms: The report of guests due to leave today.
The record of a guest's charges and payments.
The signed slip that proves a charge.
Money paid in advance, taken off the bill at check-out.
A hold on a guest's card to cover charges, which is not a payment.
A charge that reaches the desk after the guest has left.
An amount taken off the account with a supervisor's approval.
The account for charges a group or company has agreed to pay.
Paying by card on file without queueing at the desk.
A guest staying on and not leaving today.
The time by which guests must leave their room.
Keeping the room after the normal check-out time.
Leaving before the last booked night.
A guest who leaves without paying.
A room that is empty but not yet cleaned.
A record of a guest's likes, needs and stays.
The record of important matters for the next shift.
General Consumption Tax; shown at the current rate set by law.

c1.title: Ms Walters leaves a villa in Ocho Rios
c1.text: Ms Dionne Walters is checking out of a villa in Ocho Rios after three nights at J$19,500 a night. Her folio also shows a restaurant bill of J$9,200, minibar J$2,100, laundry J$1,800 and a tour J$7,500. She paid a J$20,000 deposit when she booked, and wants to pay the balance by card. The folio was checked the night before.

c2.title: Mr Spence and his company
c2.text: Mr Leroy Spence, an engineer staying at a Kingston guest house, has his room paid for by his employer, Island Ridge Works Ltd, by invoice later. The company's letter says it pays the room only. At check-out Mr Spence has run up J$14,300 for meals, drinks and laundry. He says that J$4,800 of the spa charge is not his, because the therapist did a shorter treatment than she charged.

c3.title: Mrs Daley's flight and a late check-out
c3.text: Mrs Beverley Daley wants to keep her room until 4:00 p.m. because her flight from Sangster International Airport is at 8:00 p.m. Normal check-out is 11:00 a.m. The guest house has an arrival booked for 2:00 p.m. in her room type, and other rooms are free. The policy allows a late check-out to 1:00 p.m. at no charge.

c4.title: A tour group leaves at dawn
c4.text: A tour group of 24 guests is leaving a Negril hotel at 6:00 a.m. The tour operator, Sunset Trails Ltd, pays for the rooms (one master folio); each guest pays their own drinks and spa charges. The night auditor finds two bar slips with no room number. The bell attendant has only one trolley.

c5.title: A card that does not work
c5.text: Mr Winston Pryce is checking out of a guest house in Mandeville. His bill is J$38,400. When trainee Kadian keys the amount into the terminal, it shows 'declined'. Several other guests are queueing behind him. Mr Pryce says he has used the card all week and that he has US$150 cash with him; the property's made-up rate today is US$1 = J$156.

c6.title: The empty room at 11:30
c6.text: At 11:30 a.m. Mrs Karen Blake, who is on today's departures list at a villa in Port Antonio, has not come to the desk. Her key card was left in the drop box at 6:00 a.m. Her folio shows a balance of J$12,300 and a card on file. There is a J$3,800 minibar slip on the housekeeper's cart for her room.

questions.q: What is the balance Ms Walters owes after her deposit is taken off?
Kadian charges J$79,100 to the card. What has she missed?
o: The tour, which the tour company pays for the guests
The GCT, which is paid by the villa and not the guest
The minibar, which is charged separately each time
The deposit, taken off the amount owed
questions.why: A deposit is a payment already made, so it is taken off the total before the card is charged. Charging the full J$79,100 would make Ms Walters pay J$20,000 twice.

questions.q: Kadian sees her mistake after the card has been charged. What should she do?
o: Charge the card again for J$59,100, so that the total comes right
Ask Ms Walters to claim the extra from her bank next week
Tell the supervisor, correct the card charge and apologise
Say nothing, and give Ms Walters the difference as cash from her own pocket
questions.why: A wrong amount on a card must be corrected properly, with the supervisor's help and a record, so the guest is refunded through the card. Paying cash out of your pocket or asking the guest to wait is not acceptable, and charging again would make it worse.

questions.q: While Ms Walters is paying, she says she took two bottles of water from the minibar this morning. What should Kadian do?
o: Ignore it, since the folio was checked last night
Tell her it is a late charge, to be added after she has left
Post the minibar charge to the folio before taking payment
Ask housekeeping to add it later and charge her card again
questions.why: Asking about last-minute charges, and posting them before payment, prevents late charges. Once she has paid and gone, the charge is harder to collect.

questions.q: Which charges go on the company's folio for Mr Spence?
o: Everything, as the company is his employer
The room and nothing else
The room and the spa treatment
The room, meals and laundry
questions.why: The company's letter says it pays the room only, so the room goes on the company's folio. Meals, drinks, laundry and the spa belong on Mr Spence's own folio.

questions.q: How should the desk deal with Mr Spence's complaint about the spa charge?
o: Tell him the system shows what the spa charged and that is final
Ask him to pay now and write to the spa about it afterwards
Take J$4,800 off straight away, since he is a business guest here
Check the signed voucher; ask the supervisor about an allowance
questions.why: Always look at the signed voucher with the guest first. If the charge is wrong, an allowance needs the supervisor's approval. Removing it without checking, or refusing to listen, are both wrong.

questions.q: Where does the company's folio go when Mr Spence checks out?
o: To the city ledger, with the approval letter
To the guest ledger, to wait for his next stay
Back to the spa, to be checked against its own records
To Mr Spence, to take to his employer himself
questions.why: A folio billed to a company later goes to the city ledger, with the written approval. Mr Spence settles his own folio at the desk.

questions.q: Mrs Daley asks for a 4:00 p.m. check-out. What should the agent do first?
o: Say yes, because her flight is not until 8:00 p.m.
Ask housekeeping to clean the room around her things
Say no, because normal check-out is at 11:00 a.m.
Check room availability and the policy, then reply
questions.why: A late check-out depends on whether the room is needed and what the policy says. Check first and then reply honestly, rather than promising or refusing without looking.

questions.q: If a late check-out beyond 1:00 p.m. is allowed but charged, when must Mrs Daley be told the cost?
o: When she brings the key card to the desk
Only if she asks what the charge is
At the time she settles her final account
Before she agrees
questions.why: Any extra charge must be explained before the guest agrees to it. A surprise charge on the bill leads to a dispute.

questions.q: If the room is needed at 2:00 p.m., what is the best way to help Mrs Daley with her afternoon?
o: Offer the free late check-out to 1:00 p.m., and store her bags
Keep the new arrival waiting until 4:00 p.m., so Mrs Daley can stay
Let her leave her bags in the lobby without a tag until she is ready
Move the new arrival to a smaller room, without asking the guest
questions.why: Offer what the policy allows, and help in another way by storing her luggage safely, tagged and in the locked luggage room. Making another guest wait, or leaving bags untagged, creates new problems.

questions.q: The night auditor finds two bar slips with no room number. What should be done?
o: Find out from the bar who signed them, and post to that guest
Post them to the master folio, so the tour company pays for them
Leave them out of the bills, as they cannot be traced to anyone
Divide them between guests who were in the bar that night
questions.why: A slip without a room number must be traced to the right guest, usually by asking the bar staff or checking the signature. Guessing or sharing the cost is unfair and could overcharge people or the tour company.

questions.q: At check-out, who pays for the guests' drinks and spa charges?
o: The tour leader, who settles for the whole group
Each guest, at the desk, on their own folio
The tour company, on the master folio for the group
The hotel itself, as part of the agreed group rate
questions.why: The tour company pays only what it agreed: the rooms, on the master folio. Extras belong to each guest, who settles them before leaving.

questions.q: With one trolley and 24 guests leaving at 6:00 a.m., what is the best plan?
o: Ask the guests to carry their own bags out to the coach
Leave all the bags in the lobby until the coach arrives
Wait to see who comes down first and take their bags then
Tag bags by room beforehand, and plan the trips
questions.why: A group departure needs a plan: tag bags by room, bring them down in a set order and keep the lobby clear. Waiting until the morning leads to delay and lost bags.

questions.q: The terminal shows 'declined'. What should Kadian do?
o: Ask him to leave the card and come back to pay later
Say loudly that the card is refused, so that he knows
Tell Mr Pryce quietly, and ask for another way to pay
Try the card again, to see whether it works the second time
questions.why: A declined card is private. Tell the guest quietly and ask for another way to pay. Trying again and again or embarrassing him in front of others is wrong.

questions.q: Mr Pryce decides to pay US$150 in cash towards the bill. How many J$ is that worth at today's rate?
questions.why: US$150 × 156 = J$23,400. Multiply when changing US$ into J$, and check the decimal point.

questions.q: After the US$150 is posted, how much of the J$38,400 is left to pay?
questions.why: 38,400 − 23,400 = J$15,000. Check: 23,400 + 15,000 = 38,400. The rest can be paid by another card or in cash.

questions.q: Mrs Blake left her key in the drop box at 6:00 a.m. What should the desk do about her unpaid balance?
o: Charge her card at once, whatever she agreed at check-in
Tell the other guests that she has left without paying
Wait for her to phone, and do nothing in the meantime
Check whether she agreed to express check-out first
questions.why: Express check-out works only if the guest has agreed to pay by the card on file. Check what she signed and follow the policy. If she has not agreed, report to the supervisor. Do not accuse her or tell other guests.

questions.q: What should happen to the J$3,800 minibar slip?
o: Post it to her folio before the balance is charged
Post it later as a late charge, after the folio is closed
Throw it away, since she has already left the villa
Charge it to the next guest who is given the room
questions.why: The folio is not yet settled, so the slip goes on it before the card is charged. It is better to have the full bill now than to chase a late charge later.

questions.q: If Mrs Blake's card on file is not accepted, how should she be contacted?
o: By posting a notice at the desk with her room number
By asking the next guest in her room to give her a message
Phone or email her privately, giving the balance
By telling the taxi driver she left with to pass it on
questions.why: Contact the guest directly, politely and privately, using the details she gave. Keep it confidential: never display her name or balance where others can see.

questions.q: A hurricane warning cancels flights, and a departing guest asks to stay two more nights. What is the best response?
o: Agree at once and keep the same rate for the extra nights
Tell the supervisor, and follow the property's plan
Move her to a cheaper room without asking
Say the room is booked and she must leave by 11:00 a.m.
questions.why: Extensions, rates and room changes during a hurricane warning are decisions for the supervisor, who follows the property's plan. Promising or refusing on your own may cause problems for the guest or the property.
